meta.title: How your build becomes a lesson
meta.subject: Teach
meta.one_liner: Teach turns the work already sitting in your chat into a visual lesson that stays on your computer.
meta.builder_win: You built a reusable teacher that helps non-developers understand the technology they just made.

story.title: It is a translation line, not a second builder
story.plain: The hard work has already happened in the chat. Teach reads that trail, finds the few ideas that make the build work, and turns them into a lesson source. A small builder then pours that source into one interactive web page.
story.takeaway: The chat supplies the truth; Teach changes how that truth is explained.

analogy.title: Like the guide at the end of a factory tour
analogy.body: The guide did not assemble the product. They watched the line, chose the useful stops, and explained what each machine contributed.
analogy.limit: A guide can only explain what the tour reveals. If the chat never recorded an important decision, Teach should call out the gap instead of inventing one.

visual.title: One build trail becomes one teachable story

steps.label: Build chat
steps.detail: Decisions, code changes, mistakes, and fixes already live here.

steps.label: Mental model
steps.detail: Teach separates the big idea from the supporting details.

steps.label: Local page
steps.detail: Everything is packed into a single interactive file on your computer.

story.title: Five small parts do the whole job
story.plain: Teach is not one giant application. The skill tells Codex how to teach. The lesson source holds the facts. The HTML shell decides how those facts look and move. The build script joins them. A tiny local server gives your browser a safe address to open.
story.takeaway: Keeping content separate from presentation makes every new lesson faster and more consistent.

analogy.title: Like a pop-up exhibition kit
analogy.body: A curator brings labels, a floor plan, reusable display stands, and instructions. The museum can stage a new exhibition without rebuilding the room.
analogy.limit: Unlike a physical exhibition, this page cannot see new facts after it is built. Codex must rebuild it when the lesson changes.

nodes.label: Current chat
nodes.detail: The evidence about what was built.

story.title: Local means the page stays in your room
story.plain: The finished lesson is served only on the loopback address, which is the computer talking to itself. It does not need a GrowthX account, database, model key, tracking script, or internet connection. That keeps version one easy to trust and easy to install.
story.takeaway: Local-first removes the product machinery that is not needed to learn from one chat.

analogy.title: A whiteboard in your study, not a billboard
analogy.body: You can write, erase, and learn from the whiteboard without publishing it outside your home.
analogy.limit: Someone with access to your computer can still open the file. Local does not mean encrypted or access-controlled.

visual.title: Version one and the possible hosted version solve different problems

left.label: Local v1
left.detail: A private lesson for the builder who just finished the chat.
points: Questions return to the same Codex chat

right.label: GrowthX v2
right.detail: A shareable learning product with real accounts and persistence.

story.title: A question should improve the lesson, not disappear
story.plain: The page can help the learner form a clear question, but it does not pretend to contain an AI assistant. It copies a prompt back to the chat where Codex already knows the build. Codex answers, updates the lesson source, and rebuilds the same page.
story.takeaway: Follow-up questions stay grounded because the same build conversation answers them.

analogy.title: Like raising your hand during a workshop
analogy.body: The worksheet helps you notice the gap, but the instructor answers it using the project on the table.
analogy.limit: The first version needs the learner to paste or send the copied prompt. It is not a live chat embedded in the page.

stack.summary: Teach v1 has an instruction layer, a small page builder, an editable lesson file, and a browser interface. It has no separate backend or database: everything is built and served on the builder's own computer.

items.role: The Teach skill tells Codex how to inspect the build, explain it, draw the diagrams, and define the jargon.
items.connection: Codex follows the skill and writes the explanation into lesson.json.

items.role: A short Python script checks the lesson source and combines it with the reusable page design.
items.connection: A function call gives the script lesson.json; the script returns a finished index.html file.

items.role: This file stores the explanation, diagrams, tech stack, dictionary, scenarios, quiz, and follow-up questions.
items.connection: The page builder reads it and places each named piece into the matching part of the interface.

items.role: Together these form the frontend: HTML holds the content, CSS controls the appearance, and JavaScript makes it respond to the learner.
items.connection: The browser reads the finished file and turns it into the clickable lesson the learner sees.

items.role: A tiny server gives the finished page a private address that only the same computer can open.
items.connection: It sends index.html to the browser at 127.0.0.1; nothing is uploaded to a hosted service.

concepts.plain: A reusable set of instructions that teaches Codex how to perform a particular kind of work.
concepts.in_build: Teach's skill defines the lesson workflow, teacher voice, visual rules, and local-only boundary.

concepts.plain: An installable package that can carry one or more skills and the files they need.
concepts.in_build: The Teach plugin carries the Teach skill, its brand references, scripts, icons, and HTML shell.

concepts.plain: A tidy text format for storing named pieces of information.
concepts.in_build: Each lesson keeps its title, chapters, diagrams, quiz, and follow-ups in lesson.json.

concepts.plain: A web page format that describes the content and structure the browser should display.
concepts.in_build: The generated index.html packs the lesson's content, styling, and interactions into one page.

concepts.plain: A private web address that points back to the same computer.
concepts.in_build: Teach serves lessons on 127.0.0.1 so the browser can open them without publishing them.

concepts.plain: The rules that control how a web page looks, including its colors, spacing, and layout.
concepts.in_build: Teach's CSS gives every lesson the warm paper, blue wires, cards, and responsive layout.

concepts.plain: Instructions that let a web page react when someone clicks, types, or changes something.
concepts.in_build: Teach uses JavaScript for diagrams, scenarios, glossary tooltips, the quiz, and copying follow-up questions.

concepts.plain: A programming language often used for small tools, automation, and backend work.
concepts.in_build: Teach uses Python to check lesson.json, combine it with the HTML shell, and run the local server.

concepts.plain: The part of a product that runs in front of the user and creates what they see and interact with.
concepts.in_build: Teach's frontend is the generated HTML page, styled by CSS and made interactive by JavaScript.

concepts.plain: The visible controls, words, and visuals a person uses to interact with a product.
concepts.in_build: Teach's interface is the lesson page with diagrams, dotted terms, scenarios, quiz controls, and follow-up questions.

concepts.plain: The behind-the-scenes part of a product that receives requests, runs rules, and often reads or saves data.
concepts.in_build: Teach v1 has no separate backend; Codex and the local Python tools create the page before the learner opens it.

concepts.plain: One part of a program asking a named set of instructions to do a job, often with information supplied as input.
concepts.in_build: Teach calls its Python build function with lesson.json, and JavaScript calls smaller functions whenever the learner clicks or answers.

concepts.plain: The builder assistant that can read the current conversation and work with files on the computer.
concepts.in_build: Codex uses the Teach instructions to turn the active build conversation into a lesson.

concepts.plain: The information already available from the conversation and the work around it.
concepts.in_build: Teach uses the current chat as context so the builder does not need to explain the build again.

concepts.plain: The explicit instruction used to run the Teach skill inside a Codex chat.
concepts.in_build: The lesson copies follow-up questions beginning with $teach so Codex knows to answer and improve the same lesson.

concepts.plain: An organized place where a product saves information for later.
concepts.in_build: Teach v1 does not use a database; the lesson stays as files on the builder's computer.

concepts.plain: A private credential that lets software use an online service.
concepts.in_build: Teach's local lesson does not require an API key because it does not call an AI service from the page.

concepts.plain: Page instructions that record visits or actions for analytics.
concepts.in_build: Teach v1 has no tracking script; nothing in the lesson reports how it is used.

concepts.plain: The plan for which parts a system has and how those parts work together.
concepts.in_build: Teach explains only the architecture supported by the chat and files instead of inventing missing parts.

playground.title: Change one condition and watch the teaching loop react
playground.description: Pick a situation to see where the work travels and what Teach should do next.

scenarios.label: Clear build trail
scenarios.headline: The chat contains decisions, changes, and a verified result
scenarios.body: Teach can build a confident lesson because it can connect each explanation to something that actually happened.

scenarios.label: Missing decision
scenarios.headline: The chat shows what changed but not why
scenarios.body: Teach should mark the missing reason and explain only the observed behavior. A polished guess would teach the wrong lesson.

scenarios.label: Builder asks why
scenarios.headline: A fuzzy idea becomes a useful follow-up
scenarios.body: The learner copies a focused prompt to the original chat. The answer is added to the source, and the lesson is rebuilt with a stronger explanation.

quiz.question: A lesson says a feature uses a database, but the build chat never mentioned one. What should Teach do?
choices: Keep it because most products use databases
Mark the gap and explain only what the chat proves
Publish the page so someone else can confirm it
quiz.explanation: Teach is a translator of the build evidence, not a source of invented architecture. It should make uncertainty visible and offer a focused follow-up.

quiz.question: Why does each lesson keep a JSON source as well as the finished HTML page?
choices: JSON makes the page available on the internet
JSON keeps the teaching content editable without redesigning the page
quiz.explanation: The lesson source is the editable content layer. The same visual shell can render a new or improved lesson from it.

quiz.question: A builder types a new question inside the local page. What happens in version one?
choices: The page secretly calls a model API
The question is sent to GrowthX analytics
The page copies a grounded prompt for the original Codex chat
The browser edits the source by itself
quiz.explanation: V1 keeps the lesson dependency-free and honest. The original chat already has the right context, so the question returns there.

quiz.question: Which address best matches the local-only promise?
quiz.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address: the computer is serving the page to itself rather than publishing it.
